governanceNotes: Identity-progression guard: diverticulitis is by definition inflamed diverticula, so an authoritative DIRECT_CAUSATION reading exists; the repository's conservative convention (Barrett's-to-cancer precedent) maps defining progressions as ASSOCIATION_ONLY because most carriers never develop the complication and rating pathways require the distinct diagnosis.
Progression estimates conflict by an order of magnitude across sources (1-4% JAMA 2025 vs 10-25%/5% Hawkins 2020); no progress estimate is asserted here.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The JAMA 2025 diverticulitis review states approximately 1-4% of patients with diverticulosis will develop acute diverticulitis in their lifetime, with incidence approximately 180 per 100,000 people annually (Brown 2025); the surgical update estimates lifetime risk of 10-25% with more recent studies at approximately 5% progression (Hawkins 2020); the pathophysiology review reports around 5% of patients with diverticula experiencing an acute episode while most remain asymptomatic (Piscopo & Ellul 2020).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: The inflammatory transition is the defining complication of the same anatomic disease process rather than an independent secondary condition; because only a minority of diverticulosis carriers (estimates spanning 1-4% to 5-25% depending on cohort and case definition) ever develop clinically evident diverticulitis, the mapping cannot assert individual-level causation - most diverticula never become inflamed. Graded ASSOCIATION_ONLY to preserve the distinction between the anatomic finding and the inflammatory complication, following the repository's Barrett's-to-esophageal-cancer precedent for defining-progressions.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized inflammatory-transition pathway: fecalith entrapment within a diverticulum raises intraluminal pressure and injures the mucosa where vasa recta penetrate the circular muscle; bacterial proliferation with mucosal edema and toxin accumulation produces microperforation, pericolic fat stranding, and the acute inflammatory response clinically recognized as diverticulitis. Age-related wall-structure change (elastin and collagen deposition, taeniae shortening) and low-fiber, high-red-meat dietary patterns modulate the transition, and a distinct ischemic microperforation mechanism is proposed for younger patients with sparse diverticula.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: CT-documented acute diverticulitis (contrast-enhanced CT sensitivity 98-99%, specificity 99-100%) after imaging-documented diverticulosis; Hinchey severity classification including complicated features (abscess, perforation, stricture, fistula); exclusion of colorectal cancer and other mimics by colonoscopy after the acute episode where indicated
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Contrast-enhanced CT confirming acute diverticulitis with documented preceding diverticulosis on the same or prior imaging; severity classification distinguishing uncomplicated from complicated disease; colonoscopic exclusion of malignancy and mimics after the episode where indicated
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Colorectal cancer presenting with left-lower-quadrant symptoms
Segmental colitis associated with diverticula (SCAD) and inflammatory bowel disease

evidenceGaps: Contrast-enhanced CT confirming acute diverticulitis with documented preceding diverticulosis on the same or prior imaging
Severity classification distinguishing uncomplicated disease from complicated features (abscess, free perforation, stricture, fistula) that change management and rating relevance
Colonoscopic exclusion of colorectal cancer, ischemic colitis, and inflammatory-bowel-disease mimics after the episode where age or atypical features apply
Recurrence documentation when claimed (multiple treated episodes) rather than a single episode
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: the complication is the natural-history progression of the same anatomic disease, quantified at 1-4% lifetime in the current JAMA review; an individual-level causal claim is not supportable because most diverticulosis never becomes inflamed, and the mapping preserves the source-target distinction for rating purposes.

sourceReferences.citation: Brown RF, Lopez K, Smith CB, Charles A. Diverticulitis: A Review. JAMA. 2025 Jul 24. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.10234. PMID 40705318.
sourceReferences.note: JAMA review: approximately 1-4% of patients with diverticulosis develop acute diverticulitis in their lifetime; US incidence approximately 180 per 100,000 annually with ~200,000 hospital admissions; CT sensitivity 98-99% and specificity 99-100%.

sourceReferences.citation: Hawkins AT, Wise PE, Chan T, et al. Diverticulitis: An Update From the Age Old Paradigm. Curr Probl Surg. 2020;57(10):100862. PMID 33077029.
sourceReferences.note: Surgical update: over 50% of people over 60 and over 60% over 80 have colonic diverticula; lifetime risk of developing diverticulitis estimated at 10-25% although more recent studies estimate a 5% rate of progression; the exact mechanism leading from diverticulosis to diverticulitis is not definitively known.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 33077029; progression estimates and unknown transition mechanism

sourceReferences.citation: Piscopo N, Ellul P. Diverticular Disease: A Review on Pathophysiology and Recent Evidence. Ulster Med J. 2020;89(2):83-88. PMID 33093692.
sourceReferences.note: Pathophysiology review: around 5% of patients with diverticula experience an episode of acute diverticulitis; fecolith entrapment produces mucosal damage, bacterial proliferation and toxin accumulation leading to perforation; an ischemic mechanism is proposed for younger patients with sparse diverticula.
